parameters.label: Hours in strong sun
parameters.explain: UV dose adds up with every hour in the sun — a dose is the UV strength multiplied by the time.

parameters.label: Sunscreen
parameters.explain: SPF tells you how much a sunscreen cuts the sunburn dose (when you use enough and reapply every two hours).

parameters.label: UV index
parameters.explain: The UV index measures how strong the sun's burning rays are. At 8 or more, skin is harmed quickly.

outputs.label: Time until he'd start to turn pink

overlay.caption: UV dose adds up → skin cells damaged → red hours later → darker days later

explain.summary: Sunlight carries invisible UV rays that damage skin cells. What matters is the dose — how strong the UV is times how long Kai is in it. Once the dose passes his skin's burn threshold, the skin turns red a few hours later. A few days after that it makes extra melanin, the pigment that filters UV, so his shoulders end up darker.
rules: UV dose = UV index × hours (1 UV-index hour ≈ 0.9 SED, a standard sunburn dose).
Sunscreen divides the dose by its SPF — if enough is used and it's reapplied.
Fair skin needs a smaller dose to burn than darker skin.
The more times over the threshold, the redder the skin — up to a maximum.
Extra melanin (a tan) appears 2–3 days after the damage.

source.fact: One UV-index unit is 25 mW/m² of sunburn-weighted UV (the index is that UV multiplied by 40 m²/W).
1 SED (standard erythema dose) is a sunburn-weighted UV dose of 100 J/m²; the dose that turns skin red depends on skin pigment.
The higher the UV index, the less time it takes for harm; at 8 and above you should avoid midday sun.

Sunburn's first signs may take a few hours, the full effect up to 24 hours; peeling comes several days later; fair skin burns more easily, and a very light-skinned person can burn in under 15 minutes of midday sun.
SPF measures protection against sunburn and relates to the amount of sun, not the time; reapply at least every two hours.
Delayed tanning appears 2–3 days after UV damage, and melanin filters UV.

choice.why: 25 mW/m² for 3,600 seconds is 90 J/m², and 100 J/m² is 1 SED. Real UV rises and falls through the day; we hold it steady.

choice.what: Burn thresholds of 2–8 SED by skin type
choice.why: Chosen so a very fair person burns in about 15 minutes of strong midday sun, as MedlinePlus describes, and darker skin needs more. Real thresholds vary from person to person.

choice.what: Sunscreen divides the dose by its SPF
choice.why: That's what SPF means when the amount the label asks for is used. Most people use less, so real protection is usually lower.
Beyond a few times the threshold the burn is already severe; the 0–10 scale stops there.

illustrative: Kai's six hours, UV index 8 and 'fair, burns then tans' skin are made up for a fictional story.
The 0–10 redness scale is a teaching scale.

citations.title: Measurement of Ultraviolet (UV) Index
citations.supports: The UV Index is the sunburn-weighted UV irradiance multiplied by a constant of 40 m²/W, so one UV-index unit is 25 mW/m² of sunburn-weighted UV.

citations.title: Standard Erythema Dose, a Review
citations.supports: 1 SED (standard erythema dose) is a sunburn-weighted UV exposure of 100 J/m²; the dose that makes skin just turn red varies with pigmentation and previous exposure.

citations.title: Radiation: The ultraviolet (UV) index
citations.supports: The UV index measures the level of UV radiation; the higher it is, the greater the potential for skin damage and the less time it takes for harm; at 8 and above, avoid being outside at midday.

citations.title: Sunburn
citations.supports: First signs may not appear for a few hours and the full effect can take 24 hours; pain is worst 6–48 hours after exposure; peeling comes several days later; fair skin burns more easily but dark skin can burn too; a very light-skinned person can burn in under 15 minutes of midday sun.

citations.title: Sun Protection: How to Help Protect Your Skin from the Sun
citations.supports: SPF indicates sunburn (mainly UVB) protection and relates to the amount of sun exposure, not time; higher SPF (up to 50) gives more protection; use enough and reapply at least every two hours.

citations.title: Sun Safety
citations.supports: UV rays can damage skin cells; use broad-spectrum SPF 15+ and reapply after 2 hours or after swimming or sweating; UV is strongest 10 a.m.–4 p.m. daylight saving time.

citations.title: Photoprotection conferred by low level summer sunlight exposures against pro-inflammatory UVR insult
citations.publisher: Royal Society of Chemistry (Photochemical & Photobiological Sciences)
citations.supports: States that the pigmentation in delayed tanning develops 2–3 days after UV-induced DNA damage, and that melanin acts as a broad filter reducing UV penetration.

limits.text: This is a simplified learning model. Real people vary with age, fitness and health. The numbers are illustrative, not measurements of any real person.
limits.wellbeing: Blistering, fever or feeling sick after sun is a reason to tell an adult.
